method: MIXED. S1 is the OPEN RACGP AJGP article 'Approach to palpitations' (April 2019), retrieved as HTML, tag-stripped and QUOTED VERBATIM. ITS DATE IS STATED IN THE GUIDELINE: it is seven years old and is used for the ASSESSMENT of palpitations, where it carries no drug doses, and not for drug choice. B1-B8 are eight AMH pages read under subscription and PARAPHRASED: no passage is stored and none of it is machine re-checkable. This guideline closes THREE AMH topics (Arrhythmias, Bradyarrhythmias, Tachyarrhythmias). Atrial fibrillation has its own guideline in this compendium built from the 2018 NHFA/CSANZ Australian guideline; the AF material here is AMH's and is recorded as a SECOND, INDEPENDENT source on the same questions, with the agreement on CHA2DS2-VA and on the rate-control target noted rather than merged.

claims.source_text: It is important to caution labelling a patient's palpitations as being due to anxiety/panic disorder or stress, as 54% of this group will eventually be diagnosed with an arrhythmic cause, and the time delay until arrhythmia diagnosis is 3.3 years.

claims.source_text: SVT may classically be induced by sudden movements, particularly bending. … While SVT may cause sudden light-headedness at onset, syncope is unusual.

claims.claim: A systematic review identified only SIX history factors that significantly correlated with arrhythmia: age over 60 years, regular palpitations, palpitations affected by sleep, a regular pounding sensation in the neck, visible neck pulsations, and vasovagal symptoms of pallor or diaphoresis
claims.source_text: A systematic review identified only six factors from the history that significantly correlated with arrhythmia: age of >60 years, regular palpitations, palpitations affected by sleep, regular pounding sensation in neck (atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve as in atrioventricular nodal re-entry tachycardia), visible neck pulsations, and vasovagal symptoms (pallor or diaphoresis).

claims.claim: In that systematic review the ONLY clinical sign that significantly correlated with arrhythmia was an abnormal resting heart rate, below 60 or above 100 beats per minute
claims.source_text: In a systematic review, the only clinical sign that significantly correlated with arrhythmia was abnormal resting heart rate (<60 beats per minute or >100 beats per minute).
